answer.answer: Before the change, Kubernetes shipped four releases per year, roughly one per quarter. answer.question: Why did Kubernetes move to three releases per year?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes formally reduced its release cadence from four to three releases per year. The KEP that made this change was merged on April 23, 2021.

**How it started.** The three-per-year pattern began informally in 2020 because of the COVID-19 pandemic. SIG Release made the 1.19 cycle much longer than usual to ease the load on contributors and end users. That made 1.20 the third and final release of 2020. The KEP then made this cadence official, with 15-week cycles for 1.22 and 1.23. The 1.22 changelog also says the release team had listened to users about how many releases there should be in a year.

**Underlying reasons.**
- **Growing workload.** As the project matures, each cycle includes more enhancements. That adds work for contributors and the Release Engineering team.
- **Downstream pressure.** Consumers and integrators find it harder to keep up with ever more feature-packed releases. Wider adoption means more downstream users are affected.
- **Balancing stakeholders:**
  - **Consumers and integrators** get longer support for each minor version, since the three supported releases now cover a longer period. The blog notes this is not strictly an LTS policy.
  - **Contributors** get more time to mature enhancements and make them production-ready.
  - **SIG Release** has less management overhead and only three patch releases to maintain instead of up to four overlapping. This frees time for release quality, tooling, smoother handovers between release teams, and possibly more shadows.
  - **The community** can plan upgrades and stay up to date more easily.

heading_path: The rise of Pod Security Admission
Using the built-in Pod Security Admission Controller

answer.question: What enforces pod security standards in-tree?
answer.answer:
The built-in Pod Security Admission controller (the in-tree `PodSecurity` admission plugin) enforces the Pod Security Standards. It replaces the deprecated PodSecurityPolicy.

It applies restrictions at the namespace level when pods are created. Policy is set through namespace labels, in three modes: enforce (violating pods are rejected), audit (violations add an audit annotation) and warn (violations produce a user-facing warning). Through an AdmissionConfiguration you can set cluster-wide defaults and exemptions by username, RuntimeClass or namespace.

It was alpha in v1.22, beta and enabled by default in v1.23, and stable (GA) from v1.25.

answer.question: What were Pod Security Admission's graduation stages?
answer.answer:
Pod Security Admission (the PodSecurity feature gate, which enables the PodSecurity admission plugin) went through these stages:
- Alpha in v1.22. The gate was off by default.
- Beta in v1.23–v1.24. The gate was on by default. The KEP's beta criteria included putting the admission plugin in the default enabled set, while enforcement stayed opt-in per namespace.
- Stable (GA) in v1.25. This is the same release in which PodSecurityPolicy was removed.

The feature gate stayed listed as stable through v1.27 and was then removed. An earlier version of the KEP had aimed for GA in v1.24, but the later version targeted v1.25.

answer.question: Why was PodSecurityPolicy replaced instead of fixed?
answer.answer:
PodSecurityPolicy was removed rather than fixed because the updates needed to improve its usability would have introduced breaking changes. So it was deprecated in v1.21 and removed in v1.25 in favour of a friendlier replacement, Pod Security Admission, which went Stable in v1.25.

The replacement was designed to be simpler. A robust ecosystem of external admission controllers already existed, so it did not need to cover every use case. The design focused on what a built-in controller does best: being simple to deploy and adopt. It enforces the pod security standards at the namespace level without needing deep security knowledge, and it has soft rollout features for existing clusters. It can be partly or fully deactivated so it can coexist with third-party admission controllers for more advanced cases.

answer.question: What happens to unused auto-generated ServiceAccount token Secrets?
answer.answer:
Auto-generated legacy ServiceAccount token Secrets that sit unused are first invalidated, then deleted. This is done by the legacy ServiceAccount token cleaner (feature LegacyServiceAccountTokenCleanUp), which has applied since v1.29.

How it works:
- The cleaner runs in kube-controller-manager and checks every 24 hours.
- It first checks the date in the tracking ConfigMap. This requires LegacyServiceAccountTokenTracking. If the ConfigMap is unavailable, no Secret is removed.
- If enough time has passed since that date, it looks at every Secret of type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token`.

A Secret is marked invalid if all of these are true:
- It is auto-generated, meaning it is bi-directionally referenced by a ServiceAccount.
- It is not mounted by any pod.
- It has not been used for the configured period since it was created or last used.

The last-used date is the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label if it is later than the tracking date; otherwise the tracking date is used.

Marking means adding the label `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-invalid-since` with the current date. If the invalid Secret then stays unused for another period, the cleaner deletes it.

The period defaults to one year at each step, so roughly one year to invalidation plus one more year to deletion. Admins can change it with kube-controller-manager's `--legacy-service-account-token-clean-up-period` flag.

If someone uses an invalidated token, the validator:
1. adds the audit annotation `authentication.k8s.io/legacy-token-invalidated: <secret name>/<namespace>`,
2. increments the `invalid_legacy_auto_token_uses_total` metric,
3. updates the `kubernetes.io/legacy-token-last-used` label,
4. returns an error saying the token has been invalidated.

To temporarily re-allow the token, users can remove the `invalid-since` label. The alternative is to use the TokenRequest API.

Note: earlier beta drafts of KEP-2799 (around 1.23–1.28) described deleting unused Secrets directly after the period, without the invalidation step first.

answer.question: Did Kubernetes create a token Secret for every ServiceAccount?
answer.answer:
Yes, it used to, but not any more. Before version 1.24, Kubernetes generated a Secret-based token for each ServiceAccount. In 1.24 the `LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration` feature gate became beta and was enabled by default. With it on, the Token Controller stops creating token Secrets for every ServiceAccount.

Instead, you can:
- get tokens through the TokenRequest API, or
- if you need a non-expiring token, create a Secret yourself for the token controller to fill in.

Auto-generated legacy tokens are told apart from manually created ones by whether the ServiceAccount's `secrets` field references them. From 1.29, auto-generated legacy tokens that go unused for a period (one year by default) are marked invalid. If they then stay unused for that period again, the control plane deletes them.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes stop auto-generating Secret-based ServiceAccount tokens?
answer.answer: The evidence presents this as part of a move to more secure tokens, but it never states an explicit reason for stopping auto-generation itself. The v1.29 release blog describes a sequence. By 1.22, Kubernetes had switched to more secure ServiceAccount tokens that are time-limited and bound to specific Pods. In 1.24 it stopped auto-generating the legacy Secret-based tokens. The docs add that these newer credentials come from the TokenRequest API and are mounted through a projected volume. They have bounded lifetimes and are invalidated automatically when their Pod is deleted. Kubernetes recommends this approach over long-lived Secret-based tokens. A stated motive ('to reduce potential attack surface') appears only for the later 1.29 clean-up of unused legacy tokens, not for the 1.24 change. On the mechanics: from 1.24 the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration gate was beta and on by default, and the token controller no longer created a Secret for every ServiceAccount. Users get tokens through TokenRequest instead, or create a Secret manually if they need a non-expiring token.

answer.question: Does the API server reject IP addresses with leading zeros by default?
answer.answer: It depends on the release. From Kubernetes 1.36 onward, yes: the `StrictIPCIDRValidation` feature gate is beta and enabled by default in kube-apiserver. API fields then no longer accept IP or CIDR values with extraneous leading "0"s (e.g. `010.000.000.005` instead of `10.0.0.5`). In 1.33–1.35 the gate was alpha and disabled by default. Such values were still accepted, but the API server returned a warning that they would be rejected in the future. Before that, Kubernetes deliberately kept allowing leading zeros for compatibility, as stated in 1.23, and interpreted them as decimal. The strict check applies only to fields in built-in API kinds. It does not apply to custom resources, configuration files or command-line arguments.

answer.question: Before strict IP validation was on by default, what happened when a Service used an IPv4 address with leading zeros?
answer.answer: Before StrictIPCIDRValidation became enabled by default (it was alpha and off by default in 1.33–1.35, and became beta and on by default in 1.36), Kubernetes still accepted IPv4 addresses with leading zeros. This was for compatibility, even though golang 1.17's net.ParseIP and net.ParseCIDR reject them. Kubernetes read the octets as decimal by ignoring the extra zeros, so "012.000.001.002" was treated as 12.0.1.2. Much libc-based code would instead read those octets as octal (10.0.1.2), and that difference is the CVE-2021-29923 concern. For Service IP/CIDR fields, the API server had returned warnings since 1.27 that a non-standard value like this would be considered invalid in a future release, and it suggested the canonical form. With the feature gate disabled, creating such an object still worked but produced a warning that it would be rejected in the future. Only if the gate was explicitly enabled in 1.33–1.35 were such values rejected.

answer.question: What are the release stages of strict IP/CIDR validation (KEP-4858)?
answer.answer:
Strict IP/CIDR validation, controlled by the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate, has gone through these stages:

- **Alpha in v1.33 (through v1.35):** the gate is off by default. The alpha criteria include API warnings and mandatory strict validation for `NetworkDeviceData`. They also require all kube-internal controllers to write only canonical IPs/CIDRs, with the updated validation available behind the disabled gate.
- **Beta from v1.36:** the gate is on by default. The KEP's implementation history dates this to 2026-04-22.

The latest KEP version marks itself implemented/stable, and its release checklist ticks off the GA conformance-test items. However, the evidence gives no GA release version, and the feature-gate reference still lists only alpha and beta.

When enabled, the stricter validation:
- forbids leading zeros in IPv4 octets
- forbids IPv4-mapped IPv6 values such as `::ffff:192.168.0.1`
- applies only to built-in API kinds, not to custom resources, config files or command-line arguments.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes tighten validation of IP addresses and CIDRs in API fields?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes' validation of IP and CIDR strings in API fields had historically been too lax: it accepted anything the underlying Go functions (net.ParseIP / net.ParseCIDR) accepted, even when those strings had ambiguous meanings that could cause security problems. Examples are IPv4 octets with leading 0s and IPv4-mapped IPv6 values such as ::ffff:192.168.0.1. Such values can be dangerous when different components read the same string as different IP addresses, as in CVE-2021-29923.

After Go 1.17 changed its handling of leading-zero IPs to address that CVE, there was consensus that Kubernetes API validation should eventually become stricter too. It was delayed so that existing API objects would not be retroactively invalidated. KEP-4858 laid out the plan to finally do it.

The goal is to make ambiguously-interpretable IPs and CIDRs impossible going forward, at least in new clusters. It also aims to catch malformed addresses and prefixes that previously slipped through, avoiding subtle configuration bugs, confusing runtime behavior, or security surprises.

The change is introduced through the StrictIPCIDRValidation feature gate: alpha (off by default) in 1.33–1.35, beta (on by default) from 1.36. It applies only to fields in built-in API kinds, not to custom resources, config files or command-line arguments.

answer.question: How long does a Kubernetes minor release receive patch support?
answer.answer:
Kubernetes 1.19 and newer receive approximately 1 year of patch support; 1.18 and older received approximately 9 months. The project maintains release branches for the three most recent minor releases.

As of 1.31, the patch releases page gives more detail, in line with the yearly support KEP. A patch release series is supported for roughly 14 months:
- **Standard period (first 12 months):** toward the end, Release Managers cut a release and the series enters maintenance mode.
- **Maintenance mode (2 months):** extra releases may be cut only for CVE-assigned vulnerabilities, dependency issues (including base image updates) and critical core component issues.
- **End of life:** after maintenance mode the series is EOL, and cherry picks to its branch are closed soon after.

answer.answer: The legacy Google-hosted repositories (apt.kubernetes.io and yum.kubernetes.io) were formally deprecated on August 31, 2023, and their contents were frozen on (approximately) September 13, 2023. They were actually removed on March 4, 2024, and Kubernetes packages can no longer be installed from them.

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes extend patch support for minor releases from 9 months to about a year?
answer.answer:
Because users asked for it. Business cycles (financial, certification, sales, vacation, HR and others) are overwhelmingly annual, so many users wanted support cycles of at least a year. Nine months fits poorly with most companies' planning, operations and financial cycles.

A WG LTS survey in early 2019 showed that a significant share of users did not upgrade within the 9-month window. About 1/3 had production machines on out-of-support versions. The survey suggested that support of 12–14 months would let roughly that 30% stay supported, raising the supported share from 50–60% to over 80%.

The KEP saw the extension as a relatively small change that was viable to implement and a meaningful first response to users. Keeping it small would also expose the unknowns of changing support windows so they could be addressed.

The proposal set 14 months: about 12 months of support plus 2 months for upgrading. This formalized the existing practice of keeping patch-branch CI running for 6–7 weeks past the 9 months. Release 1.19 was the first to get the year of support.

answer.question: How do I configure the kube-apiserver to use more than one authorization webhook?
answer.answer:
Use a structured authorization configuration file rather than the `--authorization-mode` flag. With command-line flags you can only enable a single webhook in the authorization chain. Multiple webhooks, a per-webhook failure policy, and CEL pre-filter rules are only available through the configuration file.

Steps:
1. Write an `AuthorizationConfiguration` file. It lists the `authorizers` in the order they should be evaluated. You can include several entries of `type: Webhook`; other authorizer types appear no more than once.
2. Give each webhook its own parameters, for example:
   - `name`
   - `timeout`
   - `failurePolicy` (e.g. `Deny`)
   - `subjectAccessReviewVersion`
   - `connectionInfo` (e.g. a kubeconfig file)
   - optional `matchConditions` with CEL expressions that pre-filter which requests are sent to that webhook
3. Start kube-apiserver with `--authorization-config=<path to file>`. You cannot combine this flag with `--authorization-mode`.

Example shape:
```yaml
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: AuthorizationConfiguration
authorizers:
  - type: Webhook
    name: system-crd-protector
    webhook:
      timeout: 3s
      failurePolicy: Deny
      subjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      matchConditionSubjectAccessReviewVersion: v1
      connectionInfo:
        type: KubeConfig
        kubeConfigFile: /files/kube-system-authz-webhook.yaml
      matchConditions:
      - expression: has(request.resourceAttributes)
  # add further Webhook entries here
  - type: Node
  - type: RBAC
```

The API server automatically reloads the authorizer chain when the file changes.

Version notes: the feature is gated by `StructuredAuthorizationConfiguration`. The docs described it as beta in 1.30–1.31. The KEP claims it is implemented/stable.

answer.question: Can I write an RBAC rule that explicitly denies a permission?
answer.answer: No. RBAC permissions are purely additive: a Role or ClusterRole only contains rules that grant permissions, and there are no "deny" rules. If you don't want a subject to have a permission, don't grant it, and avoid broad wildcard rules that could grant it automatically. Because RBAC has no negative rules, combining it with the AlwaysAllow mode (for example `--authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC`) has the same effect as `AlwaysAllow` alone, so RBAC cannot narrow it.

answer.question: What were the graduation stages of KMS v2 encryption at rest?
answer.answer:
The KMSv2 feature gate (KMS v2 API for encryption at rest) went through these stages:
- Alpha in v1.25–1.26, disabled by default. It was introduced in 1.25 as the KMS v2alpha1 API.
- Beta in v1.27–1.28, enabled by default. The KMS v2 API and implementation changed incompatibly between the 1.25 alpha and the 1.27 beta. Upgrading from old versions with the alpha feature enabled results in data loss.
- Stable (GA) from v1.29, enabled by default. The v1.29 release brought improvements in performance, key rotation, health check and status, and observability. From 1.29, the KMS v1 feature gate is deprecated and disabled by default.
- The KMSv2 gate stayed stable through v1.31 and is marked removed in the feature gate reference from v1.32 onward.

heading_path: Migration from command line arguments to configuration file

answer.question: Why did Kubernetes add a structured authentication configuration file instead of keeping the --oidc-* flags?
answer.answer:
The existing OIDC authenticator, configured through the --oidc-* flags, had limitations that users wanted to tune past, and a configuration file gives more flexibility and extensibility than command-line options. It also makes future improvements easier to deliver.

The KEP's goals list the shortcomings of the flag-based approach:
- Claim validation only checked the audience claim, and only by exact values.
- Claim mapping could pick only a single value from a single claim, plus a groups prefix; nested claims were not supported.
- Using more than one OIDC provider, or more than one client ID, required an external multiplexer such as Dex.
- Changing authenticator settings meant restarting kube-apiserver.
- There was no way to set validation rules on the final user info object.

The file-based AuthenticationConfiguration provides:
- multiple JWT authenticators at the same time;
- CEL-based claim validation and mapping;
- multiple audiences per authenticator;
- dynamic reloading without restarting the API server;
- support for providers that lack OIDC discovery, via issuer.discoveryURL.

It also improves manageability and auditability, moving away from a large set of command-line options.

The --oidc-* flags were not removed outright. They are still supported and the feature is backwards-compatible. SIG Auth recommends migrating to the file, and you cannot combine --authentication-config with --oidc-* flags: the API server reports an error and exits.

Deprecation of ipvs mode in kube-proxy

answer.question: Is kube-proxy's ipvs mode still supported, and what should I use instead?
answer.answer:
ipvs mode still exists, but it is deprecated and on a path to removal. It was deprecated in Kubernetes v1.35, and kube-proxy now logs a deprecation warning at startup when it is configured with mode: ipvs. The planned timeline: by v1.40, ipvs mode is expected to be disabled by default, though you can turn it back on with the KubeProxyIPVS feature gate. By v1.43, support is to be removed entirely.

What to use instead:
- On Linux nodes, use nftables mode. It went GA in 1.33, performs better than both iptables and ipvs, and is the recommended replacement.
- If your kernel is too old for nftables, use iptables mode, which is still the default and has improved a lot in performance since ipvs was introduced.

The evidence gives these reasons for the deprecation:
- The kernel IPVS API alone cannot fully implement Kubernetes Services, so ipvs mode still relies on iptables underneath and never handled every Service edge case correctly.
- SIG Network lacks maintainers familiar with the ipvs code.

To check which mode you're running: kubectl -n kube-system get configmap kube-proxy -o jsonpath='{.data.config\.conf}' | grep 'mode:'

answer.question: In Kubernetes 1.20, how did you turn on IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack networking?
answer.answer:
In 1.20, dual-stack was an alpha feature that you had to switch on explicitly. You enabled the `IPv6DualStack` feature gate on the relevant components and gave them dual-stack network ranges:

- **kube-apiserver:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`.
- **kube-controller-manager:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`, `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>` and `--service-cluster-ip-range=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`. Node CIDR mask sizes default to /24 for IPv4 and /64 for IPv6, set via `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv4` and `--node-cidr-mask-size-ipv6`.
- **kubelet:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"`.
- **kube-proxy:** `--feature-gates="IPv6DualStack=true"` and `--cluster-cidr=<IPv4 CIDR>,<IPv6 CIDR>`.

With dual-stack enabled, you could create Services that use IPv4, IPv6 or both, and change that setting on existing Services.

This manual step went away later. From 1.21 the gate was on by default, and 1.23 removed the flag when the feature became stable.

answer.question: When did kube-proxy's nftables mode become generally available, and what came before?
answer.answer: kube-proxy's nftables mode became generally available (GA) in Kubernetes v1.33. Before that, it was introduced as an alpha feature in v1.29, added because some Linux distributions had started deprecating and removing iptables and because nftables claims to solve iptables' main performance problems. It moved to beta in v1.31, behind the NFTablesProxyMode feature gate, which was then enabled by default. Even after GA, iptables remained the default mode; you opt in with `--proxy-mode nftables` or `mode: nftables` in the config. The mode is Linux-only and requires kernel 5.13 or later. Later, v1.35 deprecated ipvs mode and named nftables the recommended replacement on Linux. In v1.37, kube-proxy warns if the mode is not set explicitly, as part of a planned move to nftables as the default in a future release.

heading_path: Highlights of features graduating to Beta

answer.question: How did support for multiple Service CIDRs (ServiceCIDR objects) progress through its release stages?
answer.answer:
Multiple Service CIDRs support (KEP-1880, SIG Network), controlled by the MultiCIDRServiceAllocator feature gate, moved through these stages:

- **Alpha, 1.27–1.30.** Disabled by default.
- **Beta, 1.31–1.32.** Still disabled by default. To use it you had to enable both the feature gate and the networking v1beta1 API group. The feature lets admins change Service CIDR ranges dynamically with zero downtime. Before this, Service ranges were fixed by a kube-apiserver flag set at cluster creation, so expanding, shrinking or replacing them required delicate maintenance that often caused downtime.
  - Also in 1.31, users of the feature get a dual-write strategy on the ClusterIP allocators by default. This avoids duplicate IPs when skewed kube-apiservers run different allocators. You can opt out with the DisableAllocatorDualWrite gate.
- **Stable (GA), 1.33.** Enabled by default and locked. At the same time, DisableAllocatorDualWrite moved to beta, disabled by default. Users can now define the cluster Service CIDR through the ServiceCIDR API object. The changelog flags "action required" for administrators and distributions: they may want ValidatingAdmissionPolicy to stop new ServiceCIDRs from overlapping other networks, or to keep a single ServiceCIDR per cluster.

answer.question: Why did SIG Network build a new nftables backend for kube-proxy?
answer.answer:
Several reasons are given:

- **iptables is stagnating.** The default Linux kube-proxy is built on iptables. Problems with iptables led to its successor, nftables, and iptables development has mostly stopped. New features and performance improvements now go mainly into nftables. Some Linux distributions have already started deprecating and removing iptables, so doing nothing would eventually leave many users unable to use the default proxy implementation.
- **Performance.** nftables claims to solve the main performance problems of iptables. Its APIs allow incremental updates whose size depends only on the Services and endpoints that changed since the last sync. Each component also gets its own private table, so there is no global lock contention as there is with iptables.
- **Fewer backends to support.** SIG Network currently maintains both the iptables and ipvs backends. It keeps ipvs because of perceived iptables performance issues. A backend as functional and non-buggy as iptables but as performant as ipvs could let it eventually deprecate both and support a single Linux backend.
- **Code cleanup.** Writing a new backend forces a fresh look at the shared core kube-proxy code, which is not well designed. That helps the cleanup and refactoring needed for a reusable "kube-proxy library" (KEP-3786).
- **Existing projects didn't fit.** Three nftables-based implementations already existed (kube-nftlb, nfproxy and kpng's nft backend). None was suitable to adopt directly or to use as a starting point.
